exact_statement: For each positive integer k, let n_k be the least integer n>2k such that for every prime p with k<p<2k one has n mod p in {0,k+1,...,p-1}. Prove: for every real epsilon>0 there is k_0(epsilon) such that for every integer k>=k_0(epsilon), n_k<exp(epsilon*k). The stronger target is an absolute C and k_1 such that n_k<=exp(C*k/log k) for every k>=k_1.
source: https://www.erdosproblems.com/451 and repository-cached van Doorn--Tang arXiv:2606.19863
scope_notes: The residue statement is exactly equivalent to requiring that (n-k)(n-k+1)...(n-1) have no prime divisor p with k<p<2k: such a p divides the product exactly when n mod p is one of 1,...,k.
Equivalently, for every p in (k,2k) there must be an offset s_p with 0<=s_p<p-k and p divides n+s_p. This forward-multiple formulation retains the distinguished initial prefix.

The primary required target in this campaign is the still-unproved exp(o(k)) upper bound. Finite verification, a typical-translate theorem, full-period density, or a conditional CRT first-representative assertion does not count.
The heuristic product density is D_k=product_{k<p<2k}(p-k)/p, so -log D_k is asymptotic to (log 4)k/log k; this predicts but does not prove the stronger exp(O(k/log k)) target.
